claims.text: Rapid quenching of nominal FeCoNiTi produces a dual-phase microstructure containing an fcc FeCoNi matrix and a hexagonal C14 Laves phase.
The C14 Laves phase is enriched in Ti and contains Fe, Co, and Ni.
The fcc phase exhibits ferromagnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
The coexistence of the C14 phase induces antiferromagnetic coupling between the Fe, Co, and Ni sublattices and the Ti-rich Laves phase.
Antiferromagnetic exchange coupling occurs at the fcc/C14 phase boundaries.
Antiferromagnetic exchange coupling also occurs within Ti-rich sublattices of the C14 phase.
The C14 phase and its interfaces produce local strain fields in the dual-phase alloy.
The presence of the C14 phase modifies the electronic density of states relevant to the fcc phase.
Crystal structure can affect the element-resolved magnetic moments of chemically complex alloys.
Antiferromagnetic coupling reduces net spin alignment and thereby suppresses the saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
The fcc/C14 interfaces act as strong pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
The C14 phase induces magnetic anisotropy that compensates for the limited orbital moment of the fcc phase.
Exchange-bias effects at fcc/C14 interfaces impede domain-wall motion.
Local strain, exchange bias, domain-wall pinning, and induced anisotropy make the C14 phase a magnetic hardening agent.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments.
The dual-phase FeCoNiTi alloy can reach a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
The dual-phase alloy has lower saturation magnetization than single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni counterparts.
The proposed magnetic-hardening mechanism requires a continuous or semi-continuous C14 network at fcc interfaces.
Excessive C14 content may cause brittleness or loss of ferromagnetic connectivity.
